docs.title: Dynatrace AI Agent Workshop
docs.text:
Credits

This workshop was created by Henrik Rexed (Dynatrace, Is It Observable) — originally henrikrexed/dynatrace-AI-Agent-Workshop — and migrated to the Dynatrace enablement framework so it runs in the Enablement App with quizzes, checks and self-solving steps.

AI agents are evolving fast, but many organizations still struggle with rising costs, limited visibility, and unreliable performance in production.

In this hands-on workshop you'll design, deploy, and optimize cost-efficient AI agent workflows using BMAD, kagent, Kubernetes, and Dynatrace AI Observability — all inside one environment with a local Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
• Control the biggest driver of AI agent costs.
  • Build structured multi-agent workflows with BMAD.
  • Deploy AI agents on Kubernetes using kagent.
  • Secure agents with Tetragon and Agent Sandbox.
  • Monitor cost, performance, and efficiency with Dynatrace AI Observability.
  • Evaluate agents with Phoenix + dt-evals, then optimize the inefficient ones.

  1. Why — cost, visibility, reliability of AI agents in production.
  2. kagent intro — the agentic runtime on Kubernetes.
  3. Meet the platform — operators, kagent, Phoenix, the LLM backend.
  4. Deploy two agent sets — an SRE agent + the BMAD software-building crew.
  5. Secure agents — Tetragon runtime security + Agent Sandbox.
  6. Observe — Dynatrace AI Observability.
  7. Diagnose — inject a fault, let the agent find the root cause.
  8. Evaluate — Phoenix (Arize) + dt-evals.
  9. Optimize — find unused tools/skills and cut token spend.

docs.title: The model your agents use
docs.text:
The agents need a capable tool-calling model. In an instructor-led delivery the trainer runs a shared model for the room (Qwen3-32B on a GPU box) and reads out two things: a dispenser URL and a room password. In the Terminal tab, run

useWorkshopModel

and paste them when asked (the password is not echoed). You get your own, budget-capped key; your agents are re-wired to the shared model in about a minute. Without it, everything still runs on a small model inside your cluster (qwen2.5:3b) — every step and check works, but the agents' answers are slower and often wrong, so ask your trainer for the password first.

docs.text:

Module Time You need 1. kagent in 5 minutes 5 min — 2. Setup 5 min — 3. Platform install 10 min — 4. Agents & MCP 20 min — 5. Secure 20 min — (Tetragon needs a Codespace kernel) 6. Observe 25 min Dynatrace tenant (injected in the Enablement App) 7. Diagnose 40 min — 8. Evaluate 30 min Part C: nothing · Parts A/B: an LLM judge key 9. Optimize 30 min Dynatrace tenant

Running it live? The Run of show stitches the modules into one 13-step script. Stuck? See Troubleshooting.

  • 1. kagent in 5 minutes

docs.title: 1. kagent in 5 minutes
docs.text: Before you build anything, here's the mental model for kagent — the piece that turns "an LLM calling some tools" into agents you can deploy, secure, observe, and evaluate like any other Kubernetes workload.

docs.title: Why run agents on Kubernetes at all?
docs.text:
An AI agent is a loop: a model reads a goal, decides which tool to call, reads the result, and repeats until it's done. Run that loop from a laptop script and you get no isolation, no shared credentials story, no telemetry, and no way for one agent to hand work to another. kagent moves the loop onto Kubernetes, so an agent becomes a first-class, declarative object — reconciled by a controller, scheduled onto nodes, and wired into the same observability and security tooling as the rest of your platform.

The one-line definition

kagent is an agentic runtime for Kubernetes. You describe agents, models, and tools as custom resources; a controller runs them, exposes them over a standard agent-to-agent (A2A) API, and keeps them reconciled.

docs.title: The four objects you'll meet
docs.text:
kagent ships a handful of CRDs. In this workshop you only need four of them:

CRD What it is Where you'll see it ModelConfig Which LLM an agent talks to (provider, model, endpoint, secret). agents/mcp/00-modelconfig.yaml — the shared workshop-llm (DeepSeek). Agent A deployed agent: a system prompt + a ModelConfig + the tools it may call. the SRE agent and the six BMAD agents (module 4). MCPServer A tool server that runs inside the cluster (stdio or HTTP). GitHub MCP (module 4). RemoteMCPServer A reference to a tool server reached over the network, whose tools kagent discovers. the built-in kagent-tool-server, Dynatrace MCP (module 4).

Everything else — the controller, the UI, the bundled database, and kmcp (the MCP plumbing) — runs for you once the platform is installed (module 3).

docs.title: How a tool call actually happens
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    you([you]) -->|prompt| agent["Agent (the loop)"]
    agent -->|"I need to list pods"| model[ModelConfig]
    model -->|LLM picks a tool + arguments| mcp["MCP tool server<br/>(kagent-tool-server / github / dynatrace)"]
    mcp -->|returns a result| feed[Agent feeds the result back to the LLM]
    feed -->|repeat until done| agent
    feed --> answer([final answer])

Two acronyms matter:

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard for how an agent discovers and calls tools. kagent speaks it, so any MCP server — GitHub's, Dynatrace's, or your own — plugs in the same way.
  • A2A (Agent-to-Agent) is the protocol agents use to call each other. The BMAD orchestrator delegates to the analyst, PM, architect, developer, and QA agents over A2A; that's how a "crew" works when there is no Team CRD.

docs.title: Why it fits this workshop's theme
docs.text:
The whole lab is about cost-efficient agents. Because kagent makes each tool call, model call, and agent hand-off a real span emitted over OpenTelemetry (we wire this in module 3), you can see where tokens and latency actually go — and in module 9 you use that evidence to cut the waste. No runtime, no visibility; no visibility, no optimization.

You don't configure kagent by hand here

Every object above is applied for you by the functions in modules 3–4. This page is just so the YAML you're about to read makes sense. If you want the full CRD reference, see the kagent docs.

  • 2. Setup

docs.title: 2. Setup
docs.text:
Your environment is already running: a single-node k3d Kubernetes cluster inside a dev container built from the Dynatrace enablement framework image, with kubectl, helm, k9s, node, python3 and dtctl on the path.

How you got here depends on where you are taking the workshop:

Dynatrace Enablement App (recommended)

Your trainer — or you, from the training catalog — started an environment. Everything is injected for you, per learner:

  • your tenant URL (DT_ENVIRONMENT),
  • an operator token and an ingest token for the Dynatrace Operator and the OpenTelemetry gateway,
  • a platform token (DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN) for the Dynatrace MCP server,
  • a per-learner id (DT_HOSTGROUP), which names your cluster so that your data in a shared tenant is yours alone.

You create no tokens. Open the Terminal tab and continue.

In an instructor-led delivery your trainer also gives you a dispenser URL and a room password for the shared workshop model. Run useWorkshopModel and paste both (the password is not echoed); it mints your own capped key and re-wires your agents to the shared model. Run it again if the trainer rotates the password.

GitHub Codespace

  1. Create a Codespace on this repository (Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main). Choose 4-core / 16 GB or larger.

  2. When prompted, set the secrets declared in devcontainer.json (full list in .devcontainer/SECRETS.md):

    Secret Required What it is DT_ENVIRONMENT for Dynatrace https://<env>.apps.dynatrace.com DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN for Dynatrace operator token (Kubernetes monitoring) DT_INGEST_TOKEN for Dynatrace OTLP ingest: traces, metrics, logs, events DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN for the Dynatrace MCP dt0s16 platform token WORKSHOP_DISPENSER_URL + WORKSHOP_ROOM_PASSWORD optional instructor-led: both from your workshop host — exchanged for your own model-proxy key DEEPSEEK_API_KEY optional DeepSeek key — without it (and without a room password) the agents use an in-cluster model GH_PAT optional fine-grained PAT, one demo repo, for the BMAD crew WORKSHOP_PREFIX optional your label, e.g. team-alpha — derived from your GitHub user when unset

Locally (Docker)

Put the same variables in .devcontainer/.env, then:

cd .devcontainer && make start

The agents' LLM

The agents are cost-optimized for DeepSeek (deepseek-chat), reached one of three ways, first match wins:

  1. Room password — at an instructor-led workshop the host gives you a room password and a dispenser URL. At startup they are exchanged for a personal, budget-capped key on the host's model proxy; you never handle a DeepSeek key. Re-run dispenseLlmKey if the host rotates the password.
  2. Your own DEEPSEEK_API_KEY.
  3. In-cluster model — otherwise.

In the Enablement App there are no Codespace secrets: route 1 is useWorkshopModel, which asks for the URL and password in the terminal. At a trainer-led delivery the host behind them is a shared Qwen3-32B GPU box (model qwen3-32b), not DeepSeek — same OpenAI-compatible API.

When none of the first two is present — the default in the Enablement App — the platform deploys Ollama with a small tool-calling model (qwen2.5:3b) inside your cluster, and the same <prefix>-workshop-llm ModelConfig points at it. Every step of the workshop works on it; answers are slower and less sharp than DeepSeek's, which is itself a useful lesson for module 9.

docs.title: 1. Look at your cluster
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get namespaces

One Ready node. The platform namespaces (dynatrace, kagent, phoenix, tetragon, opentelemetry-operator-system, agent-sandbox, ollama) were created when the environment started — module 3 walks through each.

Check which credentials your session has (names only — values are never printed):

variablesNeeded DT_ENVIRONMENT:false DT_INGEST_TOKEN:false DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN:false DEEPSEEK_API_KEY:false

docs.title: Your workshop prefix
docs.text:
Every learner gets a short label, WORKSHOP_PREFIX. Your agents are named after it (<prefix>-sre-agent, <prefix>-bmad-orchestrator, …) and the OpenTelemetry gateway stamps it on every span as workshop.attendee, so in a tenant shared by a whole class you can always find your agents and your telemetry:

echo "$WORKSHOP_PREFIX"

You never have to set it. In a Codespace it is derived from your GitHub user, in the Enablement App from your learner id, locally it is workshop. Set the WORKSHOP_PREFIX Codespace secret to pick your own (lowercase, starts with a letter, 2–19 characters of a-z 0-9 -); an invalid value is normalised, never rejected.

docs.title: 2. The apps you will open
docs.text:
The workshop has two web UIs. Instead of port-forwards, they are published through the framework's ingress and listed by one command:

listApps
App What it is kagent the kagent UI — chat with the agents, inspect their tools phoenix Arize Phoenix — LLM traces and evaluations
  • 3. Platform install

docs.title: 3. Platform install
docs.text:
With the cluster running (module 2), meet the observability + agent platform. The manifests live under cluster/; the installers are functions in .devcontainer/util/my_functions.sh.

What gets installed

Dynatrace Operator (Kubernetes monitoring), OpenTelemetry Operator + a gateway collector, kagent (clean base — no agents yet), Tetragon (eBPF security), an Agent Sandbox isolation baseline, and Phoenix (LLM eval/trace UI).

docs.title: 1. What is already installed
docs.text:
Your environment's post-create step ran installPlatform, which installs, in order:

Component How Namespace Dynatrace Operator + DynaKube (Kubernetes monitoring, ActiveGate only) framework dynatraceDeployOperator + deployDynatrace k8s-only dynatrace OpenTelemetry Operator + gateway collector Helm + cluster/otel/collector-gateway.yaml opentelemetry-operator-system Phoenix cluster/phoenix/phoenix.yaml, published as app phoenix phoenix kagent (clean base — no agents yet) OCI Helm chart, published as app kagent kagent Tetragon Helm tetragon Agent Sandbox baseline cluster/agent-sandbox/isolation.yaml agent-sandbox LLM backend DeepSeek secret, or Ollama when no key is set kagent / ollama

Every piece is idempotent, so you can re-run any of them — or the whole thing:

installPlatform        # everything above
installOtelGateway     # or one component at a time

docs.title: 2. Verify the platform
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A                                   # everything Running
kubectl get dynakube -n dynatrace                     # Dynatrace k8s monitoring
kubectl get otelcol -n opentelemetry-operator-system  # gateway collector
kubectl -n kagent get pods                            # kagent controller / ui / kmcp
kubectl -n phoenix get pods                           # Phoenix
listApps                                              # kagent + phoenix URLs

docs.title: How telemetry flows
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    src["kagent agents / instrumented workloads"] -->|OTLP 4317/4318| gw["otel-gateway-collector<br/>(ns opentelemetry-operator-system)"]
    gw -->|observe| dt["Dynatrace tenant (OTLP ingest)"]
    gw -->|eval / trace UI| phx["Phoenix :4317"]

The gateway normalises OpenInference/Traceloop LLM attributes to OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* semconv so Dynatrace and Phoenix agree on names. There are no agents yet — kagent is a clean base; module 4 deploys the SRE agent and the BMAD crew, at which point spans start landing in both backends.

BindPlane

BindPlane (OTel collector management) is illustrated, not installed — see the walkthrough.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Tetragon not Ready — eBPF/BTF on the container node's kernel; see cluster/tetragon/README.md.
  • OTel operator hangs — it must use its self-signed webhook cert (autoGenerateCert), already set in otel/operator-values.yaml.
  • No data in Dynatrace — check kubectl -n opentelemetry-operator-system logs deploy/otel-gateway-collector; the ingest token needs openTelemetryTrace.ingest, metrics.ingest, logs.ingest.
  • 4. Agents & MCP wiring

docs.title: 4. Agents & MCP wiring
docs.text:
With the platform up (module 3), wire MCP tooling into kagent and deploy the two agent sets. Everything lives under agents/ and installs with one idempotent script.

What gets deployed

A shared workshop-llm ModelConfig (DeepSeek, OpenAI-API compatible), the GitHub and Dynatrace MCP tool servers, an SRE agent, and the six-member BMAD crew. kagent's built-in kagent-tool-server (default Kubernetes tooling) is turned on for this phase.

docs.title: The tool surfaces
docs.text:
Tool Source Agent Kubernetes / kubectl + k8s-networking built-in kagent-tool-server SRE Dynatrace (problems, entities, logs/DQL, metrics, Davis) dynatrace-mcp-remote SRE GitHub (issues, PRs, repo contents) github-mcp-remote BMAD crew

All agents share one model: workshop-llm — DeepSeek (deepseek-chat, DeepSeek-V3), chosen for the workshop's cost-efficiency theme. DeepSeek's API is OpenAI-compatible, so kagent's OpenAI provider is pointed at https://api.deepseek.com/v1 and reads the key from secret/kagent-deepseek. Swap to OpenAI or Anthropic in agents/mcp/00-modelconfig.yaml (one-line change).

docs.title: 1. The built-in Kubernetes tooling
docs.text:
kagent's built-in tools are switched on in cluster/kagent/values.yaml, which the platform install (module 3) already used:

kagent-tools: { enabled: true }   # built-in kagent-tool-server (k8s + networking)

docs.title: 2. The MCP credentials
docs.text:
The MCP servers receive their credentials at apply time; nothing is committed:

Variable Used by In the Enablement App DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN Dynatrace MCP (problems, entities, DQL, Davis) injected for you DT_ENVIRONMENT Dynatrace MCP — the platform apps URL injected for you GH_PAT GitHub MCP (BMAD crew write-back) optional — fine-grained PAT, one demo repo, Contents/Issues/PRs RW

Without GH_PAT the BMAD crew still deploys and still plans and designs — it just cannot open issues or pull requests.

Token in pod env

The GitHub/Dynatrace MCP servers receive their token as a pod env var (kagent's MCPServer env is a static map). Scope the tokens tightly and rotate them after the workshop.

docs.title: 3. Install the agents
docs.text:
installAgents

installAgents applies, in order: the <prefix>-workshop-llm ModelConfig (DeepSeek when you have a key, the in-cluster Ollama model otherwise), the GitHub and Dynatrace MCP servers, the SRE agent, then the six BMAD agents — and waits until all seven are Accepted.

Your agents carry your prefix

The manifests template their names with ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX} (module 2), and installAgents resolves it with envsubst at apply time: you get ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent, ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-bmad-*, ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-workshop-llm and ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-github-mcp-remote. kagent reports the agent name as the OpenTelemetry service.name, so your traces arrive as ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent. The built-in kagent-tool-server, the Dynatrace MCP server and the kagent namespace are not prefixed. The helpers (askSreAgent, askAgent sre-agent …) add the prefix for you.

docs.title: 4. Verify the tools registered
docs.text:
kubectl -n kagent get mcpserver,remotemcpserver
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver kagent-tool-server  -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-github-mcp-remote -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver dynatrace-mcp-remote -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get agents

Each RemoteMCPServer should be Accepted with a non-empty discoveredTools list, and all seven agents (<prefix>-sre-agent + six <prefix>-bmad-*) should be Accepted.

docs.title: 5. Send a sample prompt
docs.text:
There are two ways to talk to any agent, and they are interchangeable — both land on the same A2A endpoint and produce the same traces:

  • kagent UI — pick the agent, drop a prompt in the chat. Best for exploring interactively and watching the agent's loop unfold turn by turn.
  • A2A — a JSON-RPC message/send to the controller. Best for scripting, CI, or pasting a prompt verbatim. askAgent wraps it.

kagent UI

Open the kagent app (listApps prints the URL), pick <prefix>-sre-agent (echo $WORKSHOP_PREFIX), and paste:

List the pods in the kagent namespace and tell me if any are unhealthy.

A2A

askSreAgent "List the pods in the kagent namespace and tell me if any are unhealthy."

The raw call it makes:

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List the pods in the kagent namespace."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent

BMAD crew — a longer, multi-hop trace

With a GH_PAT, send the orchestrator a build task — in the UI pick <prefix>-bmad-orchestrator, or: askAgent bmad-orchestrator "Build a simple Todo app in <owner>/<repo>. Run the full BMAD workflow and open a PR." 900. It is optional — the rest of the workshop uses the SRE agent.

docs.title: 6. See the traces
docs.text:
Agent LLM and tool-call spans flow automatically (kagent otel.tracing, wired in module 3) through the OTel gateway to both backends:

  • Phoenix — the phoenix app (listApps) for LLM eval/trace inspection.
  • Dynatrace — distributed traces on your tenant.
  • 5. Secure agents

docs.title: 5. Secure agents (Tetragon + Agent Sandbox)
docs.text:
An AI agent is, by design, given tools and told to act. That is exactly what makes it useful — and exactly what makes it risky. A prompt-injected or mis-behaving agent will happily run whatever tool it can reach. This module adds two independent layers of defence that were installed in module 3:

  • Agent Sandbox — contain where an agent can go (namespace isolation).
  • Tetragon — observe and optionally enforce what an agent's processes do at runtime (eBPF).

Defence in depth

Neither layer replaces the other. The sandbox is a static boundary (admission + network policy); Tetragon is a runtime sensor that sees the actual syscalls/exec/network events — and can kill on policy violation. Use both.

docs.title: Part A — Agent Sandbox (isolation baseline)
docs.text:
The agent-sandbox namespace ships a self-contained isolation baseline — no external project required. It lives in cluster/agent-sandbox/isolation.yaml and enforces two things on anything scheduled into it:

Control What it does Pod Security Admission restricted Pods must run non-root, drop ALL Linux capabilities, forbid privilege escalation, and use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile. Default-deny NetworkPolicy All ingress is blocked; egress is allowed only to DNS (port 53) and the OTel gateway (4317/4318) — so a sandboxed agent can still be observed but cannot roam the cluster or call out to the internet.

docs.title: Verify the sandbox
docs.text:
# PSA labels enforce the "restricted" profile
kubectl get ns agent-sandbox -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'; echo

# the default-deny policy is present
kubectl -n agent-sandbox get networkpolicy

You should see pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted in the labels and a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Prove it actually blocks
docs.text:
Try to schedule a privileged, root pod into the sandbox — admission must reject it:

kubectl -n agent-sandbox run rogue --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"rogue","image":"busybox:1.36","securityContext":{"privileged":true,"runAsUser":0},"command":["sleep","3600"]}]}}' \
  --command -- sleep 3600

Expected

The API server refuses the pod with a violates PodSecurity "restricted" error (privileged, runAsUser=0, missing seccomp, capabilities not dropped). That's admission control doing its job — the rogue workload never starts.

Now prove the network boundary from a compliant pod:

# a compliant (non-root, no caps) pod lands, but egress is denied except DNS + OTel
kubectl -n agent-sandbox run probe --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"probe","image":"curlimages/curl:8.10.1","securityContext":{"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":65534,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}},"command":["sleep","120"]}]}}' \
  --command -- sleep 120

kubectl -n agent-sandbox exec probe -- curl -s -m 5 https://example.com || echo "BLOCKED (expected)"
kubectl -n agent-sandbox delete pod probe rogue --ignore-not-found

The external curl times out → the default-deny egress policy is working.

Stronger isolation later

The baseline is PSA + NetworkPolicy, which needs no extra controller. For runtime-level isolation (gVisor/Kata-backed pods) you can layer on kagent substrate or kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox — both are additive and don't remove this baseline. See cluster/agent-sandbox/README.md.

docs.title: Part B — Tetragon (eBPF runtime security)
docs.text: Tetragon attaches eBPF programs to the kernel to observe — and optionally enforce — process execution and network behaviour, with almost no overhead. It was installed as a DaemonSet in module 3 (cluster/tetragon/).

docs.title: Verify Tetragon is running
docs.text: kubectl -n tetragon get pods            # tetragon DaemonSet + tetragon-operator Ready

docs.title: Watch what your agents actually do
docs.text:
Stream live process/network events with the tetra CLI that ships inside the DaemonSet pod. Leave this running in one terminal, then send a prompt to the SRE agent (module 4) in another:

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact

You'll see a line for every process_exec and network connection across the node — including the processes the kagent agents spawn when they run a tool. This is your ground-truth audit log: what did the agent's container actually execute?

Filter to the interesting bits

tetra getevents -o compact --pods <pod> narrows the stream to a single pod. Pipe to grep for a specific binary (e.g. grep curl) to catch an agent reaching for the network.

docs.title: Detect an agent reading sensitive files
docs.text:
The raw getevents stream shows everything. A real audit policy says what you actually care about. For an AI agent the highest-signal thing to watch for is a process reaching for credentials — the service-account token, mounted secrets, /etc/shadow, SSH keys. That is the exact move a prompt-injected agent makes when it tries to escalate. A TracingPolicy turns "that happened somewhere in the firehose" into a single, named event the moment the file is touched.

Apply the ready-made detection policy (cluster/tetragon/sensitive-file-access.yaml):

kubectl apply -f cluster/tetragon/sensitive-file-access.yaml
kubectl -n agent-sandbox get tracingpolicynamespaced   # detect-sensitive-file-access

It hooks the kernel's security_file_permission LSM check and Posts an event whenever any process in the agent-sandbox namespace reads a path under the service-account token, /var/run/secrets, /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, the kubeconfig, SSH keys, or /home. It is scoped to the sandbox namespace so you only see agent activity — not every system process on the node reading /etc/passwd.

Why detect, not kill?

This policy uses the Post action (generate an event), not Sigkill. Detection attaches on essentially any kernel; enforcement is kernel-dependent and may be unavailable on a restricted Codespace host. You still get the full security value — you see the access the instant it happens — and the step works reliably for everyone. Flip the matchActions to Sigkill once you have confirmed your host supports it (next section).

Now trigger it. Watch the filtered stream in one terminal:

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact --namespace agent-sandbox

…and in a second terminal, schedule a compliant pod into the sandbox that reads credentials in a loop — /etc/passwd and its own service-account token, exactly what a credential-stealing agent would do:

kubectl -n agent-sandbox run snoop --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"snoop","image":"busybox:1.36","securityContext":{"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":65534,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}},"command":["sh","-c","while true; do cat /etc/passwd /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 2; done"]}]}}' \
  --command -- sh -c 'while true; do cat /etc/passwd /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 2; done'

Why a loop?

tetra getevents is a live tail — it only shows events that happen after it attaches, and never replays history. A one-shot cat … ; sleep 30 reads the file exactly once at startup, so if the pod started before your watch, the single read is already gone and you see nothing. Reading in a loop every 2 s means the trigger always lands inside your watch window — no timing luck required. /etc/passwd is a real path on the container rootfs (no symlink indirection), so it is guaranteed to match the policy's prefix; the service-account token is the realistic credential-theft target.

Expected

Within a couple of seconds the first terminal prints a process_kprobe line for security_file_permission on the snoop pod, naming the binary (cat) and the sensitive path (/etc/passwd and/or the token path). That is your detection firing — the pod ran clean under Pod Security and was caught reading a credential, because runtime detection sees what admission cannot.

No events? Check the policy loaded, not just that it applied

kubectl apply only stores the policy — the Tetragon agent still has to load the kprobe into the kernel and can silently reject it, leaving nothing to fire. Confirm it loaded before you blame the trigger: 

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra tracingpolicy list
STATE should read enabled. A load_error (or a ReturnArgAction … Post unsupported line in kubectl -n tetragon logs ds/tetragon -c tetragon) usually means a stale policy — git pull origin main and re-apply. Full ladder: Troubleshooting → Tetragon fires no events.

Clean up:

kubectl -n agent-sandbox delete pod snoop --ignore-not-found
# leave the policy in place — it is cheap and keeps watching

docs.title: Optional: enforce, don't just observe
docs.text:
Tetragon can turn an observation into a kill. A TracingPolicy can, for example, Sigkill any process in the sandbox that tries to execute an unexpected binary. This is powerful but kernel-dependent on a shared Codespace host — see the troubleshooting note below before relying on enforcement.

# Illustrative — a policy that kills shells spawned inside the sandbox namespace.
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicyNamespaced
metadata:
  name: no-shell-in-sandbox
  namespace: agent-sandbox
spec:
  kprobes:
    - call: "sys_execve"
      syscall: true
      args:
        - index: 0
          type: "string"
      selectors:
        - matchArgs:
            - index: 0
              operator: "Postfix"
              values: ["/bin/sh", "/bin/bash"]
          matchActions:
            - action: Sigkill

eBPF on a Codespace kernel

k3d/kind nodes share the Codespace host kernel. Observation (getevents) works on most hosts; enforcement (Sigkill) may be unavailable on a restricted host kernel. If Tetragon pods CrashLoop, see Troubleshooting → Tetragon.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• The agent-sandbox namespace rejects privileged/root pods and blocks egress except DNS + telemetry.
  • Tetragon streams real exec/network events from your running agents, giving you a runtime audit trail (and an optional enforcement hook).
  • A detect-sensitive-file-access TracingPolicy fires a named event the instant a sandboxed agent reads a credential (service-account token, secrets, /etc/shadow, SSH keys) — catching credential theft that admission control cannot see.

Your agents can now act — but only inside a box you drew, under a sensor that watches.

  • 6. Observe with Dynatrace

docs.title: 6. Observe with Dynatrace AI Observability
docs.text:
You now have agents running (module 4) inside a secured sandbox (module 5). But are they fast? Reliable? How much are they costing you per run? This module uses Dynatrace AI Observability to answer that — turning the spans your agents already emit into cost, token, latency, and quality signals.

Nothing to install here

The pipeline was wired in module 3: kagent's otel.tracing sends every LLM call, tool call, and agent hop as an OTLP span to the gateway collector, which forwards to both Dynatrace and Phoenix. This module is about reading that data in Dynatrace.

docs.title: How agent telemetry reaches Dynatrace
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    agent["kagent Agent<br/>(LLM + tool spans, gen_ai.* semconv)"] -->|OTLP 4317| gw["otel-gateway-collector<br/>(normalises OpenInference/Traceloop → gen_ai.*)"]
    gw -->|you are here| dt["Dynatrace tenant (OTLP ingest)"]
    gw --> phx["Phoenix (module 8)"]

The gateway normalises OpenInference/Traceloop LLM attributes onto the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* semantic conventions, so Dynatrace sees consistent gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, and token/latency fields regardless of which instrumentation a tool used.

Production tip — use the genainormalizer processor

The workshop does this with a few OTTL set() statements because it runs the lighter opentelemetry-collector-k8s image. Outside the workshop, prefer the purpose-built genainormalizer processor: it ships maintained OpenInference/OpenLLMetry (Traceloop) mappings against GenAI semconv v1.40.0. It is a contrib component (Alpha for traces), so it requires the opentelemetry-collector-contrib image or a custom OCB build.

docs.title: 1. Generate some traffic
docs.text:
Observability needs something to observe. Send a few prompts so there are runs to inspect — either way from module 4 works (kagent UI → <prefix>-sre-agent, or askSreAgent below):

generateAgentTraffic      # two diagnostic prompts to the SRE agent
askSreAgent "List pods in all namespaces and summarise anything not Running."

Run a BMAD workflow too if you have a GH_PAT and want a longer, multi-hop trace to look at.

Every one of those runs is already in Phoenix — the same gateway feeds both backends, so this check needs no tenant:

Now the same spans in your tenant. The gateway stamps every span with your cluster's name, which ends with your session id — so this counts only yours:

fetch spans, from:now()-2h
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}")
| filter isNotNull(gen_ai.request.model) or isNotNull(gen_ai.operation.name)
| summarize spans = count(), inputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens), outputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens), by:{ gen_ai.request.model }

docs.title: 2. Open AI Observability in Dynatrace
docs.text:
In your Dynatrace tenant, open AI Observability (apps menu → Observe & Explore → AI & LLM Observability, or search the app launcher for "AI Observability").

What you should see

A list of AI/LLM services and model endpoints. Because every agent shares the workshop-llm ModelConfig (DeepSeek), you'll see the DeepSeek endpoint with call volume, token usage, latency distribution, error rate, and an estimated cost per call and in aggregate.

docs.title: 3. The four questions to ask every agent run
docs.text:
Dynatrace AI Observability is organised around the metrics that drive the workshop's cost-efficiency theme. For each agent, look at:

Question Where to look What "good" looks like How much does a run cost? Token usage × model price → estimated cost per request / per service. Stable, proportional to task size — no silent blow-ups. Where does the latency go? Span waterfall: model time vs tool time vs agent-to-agent hops. Model/tool time dominates; little idle gap. Is it reliable? Error rate + failure spans (tool errors, model timeouts, A2A failures). Low, with clear error messages when it does fail. Is it efficient? Tokens per task, number of tool calls per task, retries. No redundant tool calls, no runaway token growth.

docs.title: 4. Follow a single trace end to end
docs.text:
Click into one agent request. The distributed trace shows the full loop:

flowchart TD
    send["message/send (A2A)"] --> run["agent.run — the whole loop"]
    run --> llm1["gen_ai LLM call · model=deepseek-chat · in=1.2k out=340 tokens · 420ms"]
    run --> tool["tool: k8s.list_pods · 180ms"]
    run --> llm2["gen_ai LLM call · in=1.9k out=120 tokens · 380ms"]
    run --> final["final answer"]

Each gen_ai span carries the model, the input/output token counts, and the latency — so you can see exactly which step spent the tokens. For a BMAD run, you additionally see the orchestrator's A2A hops to the analyst → PM → architect → developer → QA agents as nested spans.

Build a cost view with DQL

The Dynatrace MCP server (module 4) lets the SRE agent query this itself, but you can also open Notebooks and run DQL against the spans, e.g. sum gen_ai.usage.output_tokens grouped by agent to rank your most expensive agents. That ranking is the raw material for module 9 (Optimize).

docs.title: 5. Correlate with the rest of the cluster
docs.text: Because module 3 also installed the Dynatrace Operator in Kubernetes-monitoring mode, the agent traces sit next to your cluster topology. Under Kubernetes you can line up an expensive agent run against pod CPU/memory, restarts, and node pressure — so "slow agent" vs "starved pod" is one click apart.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• Every agent run appears in Dynatrace AI Observability with cost, tokens, latency, and error signals.
  • You can open a single trace and attribute spend to a specific model or tool call, and correlate it with Kubernetes health.
  • 7. Diagnose a broken cluster

docs.title: 7. Diagnose a broken cluster with kagent
docs.text:
You have agents running (module 4), secured (module 5), and their every run flowing into Dynatrace as cost, token, latency, and quality signals (module 6). But so far nothing has broken. The sre-agent has only answered toy prompts ("list the pods"). This module is the payoff: inject a real Kubernetes failure, ask the agent, and watch it reach the root cause — then grade its answer against a ground-truth key.

Nothing new to install

This module reuses the module-4 sre-agent exactly as-is. It already has the right surface — read/investigate tools (k8s_get_resources, k8s_describe_resource, k8s_get_pod_logs, k8s_get_events), a minimal non-destructive operate set (scale/patch/rollout), and the full Dynatrace MCP — and a system prompt that is a "Findings → Root cause → Action → Verify" SRE loop. Nothing here grants the agent new destructive power; there is no k8s_delete_resource.

docs.title: Why break things
docs.text:
You can't convince yourself an AI agent can do first-line SRE triage by watching it on a healthy cluster. You validate it the way a real on-call does: break something you understand, ask the agent, and check its answer against what you know is wrong. That is the diagnosis loop the scenarios/ directory encodes:

flowchart TD
    inject["run.sh inject <id> — a real, isolated fault lands in workshop-faults"] --> paste["paste <id>/prompt.md into the sre-agent (kagent UI or A2A curl)"]
    paste --> gather["agent gathers evidence → Findings → Root cause → Action → Verify"]
    gather --> grade["grade the answer against <id>/expected-diagnosis.md (objective key)"]
    grade --> cleanup["run.sh cleanup <id> — fault removed, zero residue"]

Each scenario ships three files: manifests.yaml (the breakage), prompt.md (the exact prompt to paste — it never names the root cause), and expected-diagnosis.md (the objective answer key). The infra scenarios sit on distinct evidence channels on purpose — logs vs. events vs. terminated-reason — so even a small model (DeepSeek-V3) can be graded without ambiguity.

docs.title: Prereqs
docs.text:
• SRE agent deployed — module 4 (sre-agent in the kagent namespace). This is the only hard requirement for scenarios 01–03.
  • (Scenario 12 only) Observe pipeline live — module 6, plus the opt-in opentelemetry-demo-light app. Scenario 12 is the Dynatrace-correlation scenario and is skippable (see the callout below).

Scenario 12 has an extra resource footprint — skippable on the minimum tier

Scenarios 01–03 are self-contained and cost almost nothing: each spins up one throwaway Deployment. Scenario 12 additionally needs the opt-in opentelemetry-demo-light astronomy-shop app deployed (and Dynatrace, to show the correlation). On a minimum 4-core / 16 GB Codespace, skip 12 and run 01–03 — you still get the full infra-diagnosis payoff. Only enable 12 if you have headroom. The platform stack is already installed (module 3), so this is a single Helm install of just the demo app: 

deployOtelDemoLight
If astroshop-lite is not deployed, run.sh inject 12 fails fast and prints this exact Helm command — nothing breaks, you're just told cleanly why 12 is unavailable.

List what's available any time:

bash scenarios/run.sh list     # id, title, and an [app-dep: astroshop-lite] tag on #12

docs.title: Walkthrough — scenario 01, CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text: The rest of this page walks the canonical "hello world" of k8s diagnosis end to end. Scenarios 02 (ImagePullBackOff) and 03 (OOMKilled) follow the exact same four steps — just swap the id and paste that scenario's prompt.md.

docs.title: 1. Inject the fault
docs.text:
injectScenario 01      # = bash scenarios/run.sh inject 01-crashloopbackoff

run.sh creates the dedicated workshop-faults namespace and applies the fault's manifests.yaml. A fail-closed allowlist rejects any manifest that references kagent, dynatrace, the module-5 agent-sandbox, or any platform namespace before anything is applied — the blast radius is one throwaway namespace. Watch it break:

kubectl get pods -n workshop-faults

NAME                              READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
billing-worker-5c9f8d7b6c-ab12x   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4          90s

docs.title: 2. Ask the agent
docs.text:
Open each scenario's prompt.md and paste the prompt exactly — it describes the symptom and asks for evidence, but it never tells the agent the root cause. For scenario 01 (scenarios/01-crashloopbackoff/prompt.md):

Terminal

diagnoseScenario 01      # sends scenarios/01-crashloopbackoff/prompt.md over A2A

kagent UI

Open the kagent app (listApps), pick <prefix>-sre-agent, and paste:

A pod in the workshop-faults namespace keeps restarting. Investigate what is wrong with the workload there, find the root cause, and tell me the exact evidence (status, events, and logs) that supports it.

A2A (curl)

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"A pod in the workshop-faults namespace keeps restarting. Investigate the workload there, find the root cause, and cite the exact status, events, and log lines that support it."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent

The agent will walk its SRE loop live: list the pods, describe the failing one, pull its events and logs, and converge on a conclusion.

docs.title: 3. Grade it
docs.text:
Open the scenario's expected-diagnosis.md — the objective answer key — and check the agent's conclusion against it. Scenario 01's key wants the agent to:

  • report billing-worker in CrashLoopBackOff;
  • cite the non-zero exit code (1) from lastState.terminated;
  • quote the Back-off restarting failed container event;
  • quote the fatal log line (BILLING_DB_URL is not set);
  • conclude the start command fails on launch.

The key also lists a pass_threshold (how many signals must be cited) and a Must NOT claim section that catches small-model confabulation — e.g. for the crash-loop, claiming an ImagePullBackOff (scenario 02) or OOMKilled (scenario 03) is an unambiguous fail, because those are different evidence channels. That cross-channel discipline is why the diagnosis is graded objectively.

The same key is machine-readable (evals/ground-truth/), so you can grade the agent's answer you just got with one command:

gradeLiveDiagnosis 01

It prints the signals cited, whether the root cause was named, and PASS or FAIL. A FAIL is a result, not an error — on the small in-cluster model it is common, and it is exactly what modules 8 and 9 are about.

Each infra scenario exercises a different sense

01 reads logs, 02 reads events (Failed to pull image — no logs exist yet, so a logs-only agent is stuck), and 03 reads lastState.terminated.reason: OOMKilled (it looks like a crash loop until you check why it was killed). Running all three proves the agent reads the right signal for each failure class, not just one trick.

docs.title: 4. (Optional) Remediate & verify
docs.text:
Ask the agent for the minimal safe fix, then watch it act within its non-destructive operate set:

You found the root cause. Propose and apply the minimal, safe fix, then verify the pod reaches a healthy state.

For scenario 01 that means supplying the missing configuration (or correcting the start command) and rolling out the Deployment — k8s_patch_resource + k8s_rollout, never a delete. Re-run kubectl get pods -n workshop-faults and confirm the pod goes Running. The agent can only patch/apply/scale/rollout, so this stays safe by construction.

docs.title: 5. Cleanup
docs.text:
cleanupScenario 01     # deletes the workshop-faults ns — zero residue

Cleanup is one command and idempotent. For infra scenarios it deletes exactly the workshop-faults namespace; it never touches kagent, dynatrace, the demo app, or any platform namespace.

docs.title: The Dynatrace money shot — scenario 12 (optional)
docs.text:
Scenarios 01–03 are diagnosable from cluster state alone. Scenario 12 is the one that shows off the workshop's real differentiator: the agent correlating Kubernetes with Dynatrace. A faulty product-catalog backend joins the product-catalog Service's endpoints, so a fraction of the astronomy shop's product requests are load-balanced to it and fail — intermittent 5xx, not a clean outage.

bash scenarios/run.sh inject 12      # adds a faulty product-catalog backend (via inject.sh)

Paste scenarios/12-intermittent-5xx/prompt.md and point the agent at Dynatrace:

Users of the astronomy shop (namespace astroshop-lite) are seeing intermittent errors when they browse products — some requests work, some fail. Use Dynatrace to find the open problem and its Davis root cause, correlate it with the cluster state, and tell me which service is actually at fault and why.

A correct answer cites an open Dynatrace problem on the product path, names product-catalog as the Davis root-cause entity (not the frontend that merely surfaces it), notes the failures are intermittent (a partial error rate), and corroborates with k8s that the product-catalog Service has an extra, unhealthy backend in rotation. Grade against its expected-diagnosis.md (pass_threshold: 4). Clean up with:

bash scenarios/run.sh cleanup 12     # removes only the faulty backend — never the healthy demo

docs.title: So what — these runs feed the rest of the workshop
docs.text:
This module isn't a detour; it's the fuel for everything after it.

Every diagnosis run you just made is reusable evidence

  • Eval fixtures for 8 — Evaluate: each expected-diagnosis.md doubles as ground truth — the same Required signals / Must NOT claim keys become the scoring rubric for Phoenix and dt-evals. You now have real, labelled traces to grade, not toy prompts.
  • Cost data for 9 — Optimize: every run emitted gen_ai.* spans with token, cost, and latency. A diagnosis is a realistic, multi-tool task — exactly the kind of run whose token spend module 9 teaches you to cut without losing accuracy.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• You injected a real, isolated Kubernetes fault and the module-4 sre-agent reached the correct root cause, citing the exact signals.
  • You graded its answer objectively against expected-diagnosis.md, and (optionally) watched it remediate within its non-destructive tool set.
  • Cleanup left zero residue — the platform and module-5 isolation boundary were never touched.

Next: 8 — Evaluate (Phoenix + dt-evals) — you diagnosed and graded by hand here; now turn those answer keys into an automated eval suite.

docs.title: 8. Evaluate (Phoenix + dt-evals)
docs.text:
Observability (module 6) tells you what the agent did and what it cost. It does not tell you whether the answer was correct, grounded, or useful. That's evaluation — scoring agent outputs against expectations — and it's the step most teams skip, which is why their agents quietly regress.

This module's evals read the same gen_ai.* spans the OTel gateway already produces (module 4/6) — you don't re-run the agents to grade them, you grade the traces they already emitted. You create your evaluation in Arize Phoenix:

  • Phoenix (Arize) — the recommended path. An interactive trace + eval UI, already running from module 3, where you build and run an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation entirely in the web UI — no code.
  • dt-evals — a short alternative for teams that want eval scores to land inside Dynatrace as bizevents, next to the rest of their telemetry.
  • The diagnosis grader (Part C) — deterministic, needs no model at all.

Everything for this module lives under evals/. The judge is the workshop model — DeepSeek (deepseek-chat), the same model that powers the agents, reached through the room-password proxy or your own DEEPSEEK_API_KEY (module 2). Nothing to configure: the key is picked up from your terminal.

No LLM key in your session?

The Enablement App runs the agents on the in-cluster model and provides no judge key. Read Parts A and B, then run Part C, which grades deterministically and needs nothing.

Generate traffic first

Evals score real traces. Drive the SRE agent or a BMAD task (module 4) before running either path, so there are spans to grade.

docs.title: Part A — Phoenix: create an evaluation in the UI
docs.text:
Open the phoenix app (listApps prints its URL).

Every agent run shows up as an LLM trace: prompt, response, tool spans, token counts. Click a span to see its gen_ai.* attributes. The OTel gateway also copies each LLM call's prompt and completion onto the span as OpenInference input.value / output.value, so the Input and Output are visible right in the trace view — which is exactly what the judge reads.

The DeepSeek judge is already wired

When your session has a model key, Phoenix is preconfigured for DeepSeek: the key and endpoint are injected from your environment (secret/phoenix-deepseek) and PHOENIX_ALLOWED_PROVIDERS=DEEPSEEK restricts the model menu, so DeepSeek is the only — and obvious — choice wherever you pick a judge model. You never hand-enter a key. After a room-password rotation run dispenseLlmKey, then installPhoenix.

docs.title: Create and run an LLM-as-a-judge (no code)
docs.text:
You'll score the SRE-agent traces from your last run with a judge classifier — hallucination (is the answer grounded in the tool output it was given?) or relevance (does it answer the question?).

  1. Pick the traces. Open the Traces table and filter to the LLM spans so each example carries a clean question → answer pair — paste this into the filter bar:

    span_kind == 'LLM'

    Phoenix is per learner, so this is all the scoping you need. (The spans also carry workshop.attendee and your agents' names carry your WORKSHOP_PREFIX — that matters in a shared Dynatrace tenant, not here.)

  2. Capture them as a dataset. Select the spans and use Add to Dataset — each example keeps the span's Input (the question) and Output (the agent's answer).

  3. Add an LLM evaluator. Open the dataset → Evaluators → Add evaluator → LLM. Phoenix opens it in the Playground:
    • Model: DeepSeek (already keyed).
    • Template: the judge prompt, e.g. "You are grading whether the ANSWER is grounded in the provided CONTEXT/question. Reply with a single label: hallucinated or factual." (or a relevance rubric: relevant / irrelevant).
    • Input mapping: map the template's {question} / {answer} variables to the dataset's input / output fields.
    • Test it on one example, then Save.
  4. Run it. From the dataset, Run an experiment. Phoenix calls the judge server-side over every example.

The results table gains one label / score column per evaluator. Sort by it to surface the weakest answers, and click a row to read the judge's label and explanation next to the input and output.

docs.title: Script the same judge instead (optional)
docs.text:
The repo also ships a small, version-pinned script that builds the same two classifiers from code — handy for CI, for grading the live spans in place, or when you have no traffic yet:

cd evals && uv sync
# Bundled sample dataset — no cluster/traffic needed (just a judge key):
uv run python phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py
# Live LLM spans pulled from Phoenix, scores logged back onto the traces:
uv run python phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py --from-phoenix

It prints a per-metric summary, writes phoenix/out/phoenix_eval_results.csv, and (with --from-phoenix) annotates the originating spans so the labels show up on the traces in the UI. --from-phoenix filters server-side to span_kind == 'LLM' before its row limit, so the agents' sparse LLM spans are not buried under the demo app's infrastructure spans. Details: evals/phoenix/README.md.

--from-phoenix needs message content on the spans

The live path maps prompt/response content out of every shape these agents emit — OTel GenAI semconv (gen_ai.input.messages, indexed gen_ai.prompt.N.content / gen_ai.completion.N.content, or gen_ai.* log-events) and OpenInference (input.value / output.value). If it finds no content it prints exactly which attributes.* were present. The bundled dataset path always works offline.

docs.title: Part B — dt-evals: scores inside Dynatrace (optional)
docs.text:
dt-evals is a config-driven CLI that samples gen_ai.* spans from your Dynatrace environment, scores each with an LLM judge, and writes gen_ai.evaluation.result bizevents back — so a low score is one click from the trace, prompt, and tool calls that caused it. Where Part A had you create an evaluation by clicking, here the config file is the evaluation.

flowchart LR
    spans["Dynatrace gen_ai.* spans"] --> evals["dt-evals (sample → mask → judge)"]
    evals --> biz["bizevents"]
    biz --> out["DQL / dashboard / alert"]

The config is the evaluation. Open evals/dt-evals/workshop-agents.dt-eval.yaml. Four blocks define it — grade what, judged by whom, scored on which metrics, failing when:

Block What you declare Authoring question scope which spans to pull (service, since, sampling) What do I grade? judge the LLM-as-a-judge (DeepSeek, OpenAI-compatible) Who grades it? metrics.enabled relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, coherence, toxicity, prompt-injection What am I scoring for? alerts.thresholds the pass/fail bar per metric that makes the run exit non-zero When does it fail?

Author it in two edits: DT_EVAL_SERVICE fills scope.service (it defaults to ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent, your SRE agent), and tightening an alerts.thresholds line — e.g. relevance: 0.8 — sets the gate.

Credentials (in evals/.env, copy from evals/.env.example): a Dynatrace token with storage:spans:read + storage:events:write as DYNATRACE_API_TOKEN; the tenant URL comes from DT_ENVIRONMENT. The judge key is picked up from your session (room-password proxy or DEEPSEEK_API_KEY) — see .devcontainer/SECRETS.md and TODO-HENRIK §8 for the open question on the token type.

cd evals/dt-evals
./run-dt-eval.sh                     # renders the config, then validate + run

The run exits non-zero on a threshold breach — a ready-made CI gate. Read the scores back in a Dynatrace Notebook (replace <prefix> with echo $WORKSHOP_PREFIX):

fetch bizevents
| filter event.type == "gen_ai.evaluation.result"
| filter service.name == "<prefix>-sre-agent"
| summarize avg(toDouble(gen_ai.evaluation.score.value)), by: { gen_ai.evaluation.name }

The service.name clause scopes the read-back to your results in a shared tenant. Details: evals/dt-evals/README.md.

docs.title: Part C — grade a diagnosis against the answer key
docs.text:
Parts A/B judge generic quality (grounded? relevant? toxic?). The diagnostic module (7 — Diagnose) asks a sharper question: when the SRE agent investigates a real injected fault, did it reach the right root cause? Each scenario ships an objective answer key — scenarios/<id>/expected-diagnosis.md — and those keys are registered as this module's diagnosis-grading ground truth under evals/ground-truth/.

The grading check:

Did the diagnosis cite ≥ pass_threshold of the answer key's required signals (root cause + evidence channel), identify the root cause, and avoid the forbidden cross-channel claims?

Because scenarios 01–03 sit on distinct evidence channels (logs vs. events vs. OOMKilled status), a cross-channel claim is an unambiguous fail — so this grades objectively, even with no judge model.

docs.title: Deterministic grade (offline, no key)
docs.text:
runDiagnosisEval       # = cd evals && python3 phoenix/run_diagnosis_eval.py

The bundled dataset holds, for every scenario, one golden diagnosis and one confabulated one (plausible, wrong channel). A grader that works must pass the first and fail the second — four PASS, four FAIL. It prints the verdict per diagnosis and writes phoenix/out/diagnosis_eval_results.csv.

Add --llm-judge (needs a judge key) to also run an LLM root-cause grader, or --from-phoenix to grade the agent's live diagnosis spans and annotate them back onto the traces.

docs.title: Author a custom evaluator in Dynatrace (dt-evals — optional)
docs.text:
The sharpest form of authoring is a rubric that encodes exactly what a correct diagnosis of one scenario must say. Each answer key is compiled into one.

1. Read the rubric. Open evals/dt-evals/evaluators/diagnosis-01-crashloopbackoff.md. Its Judge prompt section is the evaluator — binary (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) with three clauses: identify the root cause, cite ≥ 3 required signals, and make none of the must-not-claim cross-channel confabulations. That required-signals + must-not-claim shape is the pattern for any objective grader. (Generated from the answer key with uv run python dt-evals/gen_diagnosis_evaluators.py — don't hand-edit.)

2. Register it, enable it, run it. Uncomment its line under metrics.enabled (and the matching alerts.thresholds) in scenario-diagnosis.dt-eval.yaml, then:

cd evals/dt-evals
./run-dt-eval.sh evaluators add      # paste the Judge prompt of evaluators/diagnosis-<id>.md
./run-dt-eval.sh --config scenario-diagnosis.dt-eval.yaml --metric diagnosis-<id>

./run-dt-eval.sh evaluators add is a passthrough to the pinned dt-evals CLI. Correct diagnoses score 1, misses 0 — a per-scenario pass/fail bizevent next to the trace. Details: evals/ground-truth/README.md.

Closing the diagnose → evaluate → optimize loop

The same diagnosis runs you grade here emit the gen_ai.* spans whose token/cost/latency drive 9 — Optimize. Break it (7 — Diagnose), grade it (8), cut the waste (9).

docs.title: What to measure for these agents
docs.text: Agent Good eval questions SRE agent Did it correctly identify the unhealthy pod? Did it call the right k8s/Dynatrace tool (not guess)? Was the diagnosis grounded in real tool output (no hallucinated pod names)? BMAD crew Did the workflow produce the expected artifacts (issues → branch → PR)? Did the developer agent stay within its repo scope? Did it finish within a token budget?

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• You created an evaluation in the Phoenix UI (dataset → evaluator → judge) and read its labelled scores — or scored the bundled dataset from code.
  • (Optional) You saw the same evaluation authored as a dt-evals config, with the scores landing in Dynatrace as queryable bizevents and a CI-friendly gate.
  • A diagnosis-grading run (Part C) scores an SRE-agent diagnosis against a scenario answer key — PASS/FAIL against registered ground truth, offline or in Dynatrace.

Next: 9. Optimize — now that you can measure cost and quality, go cut the waste.

docs.title: 9. Optimize
docs.text:
This is where the whole workshop pays off. You can now run agents (4), secure them (5), observe their cost (6), and evaluate their quality (8). Optimization is the loop that uses that evidence to make agents cheaper without making them worse.

The core idea

The biggest driver of AI agent cost is tokens — and most token spend is waste: unused tools inflating every prompt, oversized system prompts, chatty multi-hop workflows, and retries. You can't cut what you can't see, which is why observation and evaluation came first.

docs.title: The optimization loop
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    observe["observe (6)"] --> waste["find the waste"]
    evaluate["evaluate (8)"] --> change["make one change"]
    waste --> change
    change --> remeasure["re-measure cost + quality"]
    remeasure -->|keep only if quality holds| waste

Change one thing, re-run the eval suite, and keep the change only if quality holds and cost dropped. Never optimize on cost alone — that's how you ship a cheap agent that gives wrong answers.

Three ready-made surfaces — deploy them first

This module ships a Dynatrace read-the-run notebook, a dashboard and a before/after notebook that compute every signal below from your crew's gen_ai.* spans. Their DQL filters on workshop.attendee == "${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}" (module 2), so render them with your prefix, then deploy:

renderOptimizationAssets      # -> .rendered/optimization/ (YAML for dtctl, JSON for the UI)
deployOptimizationAssets      # dtctl: read-the-run notebook, dashboard, before/after notebook

No platform token in your session? Upload the rendered .json files from .rendered/optimization/ in your tenant (Notebooks / Dashboards / Workflows → Upload). The unrendered originals are in docs/assets/optimization/ — find/replace ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX} with your prefix before uploading those.

  • Notebook — Read an AI Agent Run (ai-agent-workflow-steps): walks one run from the crew list down to the per-hop token bill. Start here.
  • Dashboard — AI Agent Optimization: spend ranking, input:output ratio, tool calls, tool coverage, loop detection, token trend.
  • Notebook — AI Agent Optimization — before/after: the observe → find → change → re-measure → keep/revert walkthrough, one runnable DQL cell per step.

All five artifacts (plus the guardian and workflow of §4) are dtctl-ready YAML in cluster/dynatrace/optimization/ with a README.

docs.title: Read the workflow before you cut it
docs.text:
Before you cut an agent's cost you have to read what it is doing. The ranking and cuts below act on numbers; this section is how you earn the right to trust those numbers — by walking one real run from the outside in, zooming one level at a time:

flowchart TD
    s1["1 · Who is in the crew"] --> s2["2 · What operations an agent performs"]
    s2 --> s3["3 · Anatomy of one task"]
    s3 --> s4["4 · The A2A hand-offs"]
    s4 --> s5["5 · The reasoning loop"]
    s5 --> s6["6 · The tool-call sequence"]
    s6 --> s7["7 · Token accumulation across the run"]

Run these in your own tenant

All seven queries below are the cells of the read-the-run notebook, ai-agent-workflow-steps.notebook.yaml (deploy it from the callout above). Each step below names the matching notebook section so you can run it against your own crew and page through the run live.

First, the vocabulary these queries use — correct it to whatever your crew emits:

  • An LLM call (the agent reasoning) is a span with gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content". Key on that operation, never on a framework span name — some SDK layers wrap each call in an extra span, and the operation counts each LLM call exactly once.
  • A tool call (the agent acting) is gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool", with the tool name in gen_ai.tool.name. Drop gen_ai.tool.name == "(merged tools)" — a Dynatrace span-merge artifact, not a real tool.
  • Tokens live on gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / gen_ai.usage.output_tokens (carried on the generate_content spans).
  • One agent's unit of work is gen_ai.task.id (it stays inside a single service). A full cross-agent run is trace.id — one trace spans the whole crew.
  • Order events by start_time (timestamp is null on these spans).

Scope every query to your data

The snippets below filter on endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") — your per-learner cluster name, which the OpenTelemetry gateway stamps on every span (the Enablement App fills in the id; in a Codespace use the value aiwPrefixBanner prints). The deployed notebook and dashboard filter on the equivalent workshop.attendee == "<your prefix>". Drop the filter and a shared tenant mixes the whole class's data.

docs.title: 1 · Who is in the crew
docs.text:
What you're seeing: your agents. Every service in the kagent namespace that actually makes an LLM call is an agent (the llmCalls > 0 filter drops the kagent-controller plumbing). llmCalls is how often it reasoned; toolCalls how often it acted.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent"
| summarize spans = count(),
    llmCalls = countIf(gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"),
    toolCalls = countIf(gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool" and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"),
    by:{agent = service.name}
| filter llmCalls > 0
| sort llmCalls desc

Notebook: section 1.

docs.title: 2 · What operations an agent performs
docs.text:
What you're seeing: the vocabulary. Everything an agent emits falls into a handful of activities — it reasons (generate_content), acts (execute_tool), and talks to other agents (a2a.* + invoke_agent). Everything else is the Other bucket you can ignore while reading the run.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent"
| fieldsAdd activity = if(gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content", "LLM call (generate_content)",
    else: if(gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool", "Tool call (execute_tool)",
    else: if(gen_ai.operation.name == "invoke_agent", "Agent invocation (invoke_agent)",
    else: if(startsWith(span.name, "a2a."), "A2A messaging",
    else: "Other (HTTP / framework)"))))
| summarize spans = count(), by:{activity}
| sort spans desc

Notebook: section 2.

docs.title: 3 · Anatomy of one task
docs.text:
What you're seeing: one run, step by step. The sub-query picks the task with the most generate_content hops (the busiest reasoning loop — the most interesting example) and joins its spans back on gen_ai.task.id. Read top-to-bottom: an LLM call, then the tools it decided to run, then the next LLM call. kagent__NS__<agent> tools are hand-offs to sub-agents (see step 4).

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent"
| join [
    fetch spans
    | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"
    | summarize hops = count(), by:{gen_ai.task.id}
    | sort hops desc, gen_ai.task.id asc
    | limit 1
  ], on:{gen_ai.task.id}, kind:inner, fields:{}
| filter gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content" or gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool"
| filter gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)" or isNull(gen_ai.tool.name)
| fieldsAdd durationMs = duration / 1000000
| fields start_time, agent = service.name, step = span.name, operation = gen_ai.operation.name, durationMs
| sort start_time asc

Notebook: section 3.

docs.title: 4 · The A2A hand-offs
docs.text:
What you're seeing: the workflow graph. In this crew an agent delegates to another by calling it as a tool named kagent__NS__<agent>; stripping that prefix gives the edge fromAgent → toAgent. Hand-offs cross service.name, so they are correlated by trace.id, not by a single gen_ai.task.id. The orchestrator is usually the hub that fans work out to the specialists.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool"
| filter startsWith(gen_ai.tool.name, "kagent__")
| fieldsAdd callee = replaceString(gen_ai.tool.name, "kagent__NS__", "")
| summarize handoffs = count(), by:{fromAgent = service.name, toAgent = callee}
| sort handoffs desc

Returns nothing? That's expected unless the BMAD crew has run

A2A hand-offs (kagent__NS__<agent> tool calls) are only emitted when the <prefix>-bmad-orchestrator delegates to its specialists. The solo <prefix>-sre-agent — the default k8s-only investigation path — calls only kagent-tool-server tools and produces zero kagent__ spans by design, so this graph is empty until the crew has run. To populate it:

  1. Run the BMAD crew (the A2A sample prompt from module 4 §5) and re-run the query.
  2. Check the timeframe — the notebook cell is hard-coded to now()-7d; widen it or re-run after the crew has executed within the window.
  3. Confirm any kagent__ spans exist at all: 
    fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and startsWith(gen_ai.tool.name, "kagent__")
| summarize count(), by:{gen_ai.tool.name}
    No rows means no crew hand-offs have happened yet.

Notebook: section 4.

docs.title: 5 · The reasoning loop
docs.text:
What you're seeing: where a loop re-reads context. Same busiest task as step 3, but only its generate_content hops in order. Watch inputTokens climb hop after hop while outputTokens stays small: every hop re-sends the whole growing conversation back to the model. A flat line means a tight agent; a staircase means a context that never gets trimmed. That growth is exactly the chatty-workflow lever in §2c below.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"
| join [
    fetch spans
    | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"
    | summarize hops = count(), by:{gen_ai.task.id}
    | sort hops desc, gen_ai.task.id asc
    | limit 1
  ], on:{gen_ai.task.id}, kind:inner, fields:{}
| fields start_time, agent = service.name, inputTokens = gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, outputTokens = gen_ai.usage.output_tokens
| sort start_time asc

Notebook: section 5.

docs.title: 6 · The tool-call sequence
docs.text:
What you're seeing: what the agent decided to do. Same busiest task, now only its execute_tool spans in order. Each row is a decision the model made between reasoning hops — a memory lookup, a sub-agent delegation (kagent__NS__*), a diagnostic call. Compare this list against each agent's granted tools: tools that never appear here are the never-called overhead you drop in §2a below.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool" and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"
| join [
    fetch spans
    | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"
    | summarize hops = count(), by:{gen_ai.task.id}
    | sort hops desc, gen_ai.task.id asc
    | limit 1
  ], on:{gen_ai.task.id}, kind:inner, fields:{}
| fieldsAdd durationMs = duration / 1000000
| fields start_time, agent = service.name, tool = gen_ai.tool.name, durationMs
| sort start_time asc

Notebook: section 6.

docs.title: 7 · Token accumulation across the run
docs.text:
What you're seeing: the bill, built one hop at a time. Same busiest task, every generate_content hop with its inputTokens, outputTokens, and hopCost (the two added). Sum the inputTokens column and you get the run's input bill — on the reference tenant that was ~182k input vs ~14k output across 10 hops (≈13:1), with the last hop costing several times the first purely because the context grew. That is why trimming the loop (step 5) beats trimming almost anything else.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"
| join [
    fetch spans
    | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and gen_ai.operation.name == "generate_content"
    | summarize hops = count(), by:{gen_ai.task.id}
    | sort hops desc, gen_ai.task.id asc
    | limit 1
  ], on:{gen_ai.task.id}, kind:inner, fields:{}
| fieldsAdd hopCost = gen_ai.usage.input_tokens + gen_ai.usage.output_tokens
| fields start_time, inputTokens = gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, outputTokens = gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, hopCost
| sort start_time asc

Notebook: section 7.

With the run read end-to-end, you now know which agent to rank first and why its tokens are high. That is the ranking the rest of this page acts on.

docs.title: 1. Rank your agents by spend
docs.text:
From Dynatrace AI Observability (module 6), find your most expensive agents — total tokens and estimated cost per run. Start at the top of that list; a 20% cut on your priciest agent beats a 50% cut on a rarely-used one.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(),
    inputTokens  = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens),
    outputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens),
    by:{agent = service.name}
| fieldsAdd totalTokens = inputTokens + outputTokens,
    inOutRatio      = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / outputTokens, decimals: 1),
    avgInputPerCall = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / llmCalls)
| sort totalTokens desc

What this looked like on the reference tenant (7-day window)

Agent Total tokens in:out ratio Avg input / call seta_sre_investigator 46.2 M 38 : 1 33,180 bmad_orchestrator 11.8 M 14 : 1 8,762 bmad_developer 2.7 M 3 : 1 6,191

The whole crew burned 64 M tokens, and one agent — the SRE investigator — is 72% of it. Note the input : output ratio: 38 input tokens for every output token means the model re-reads a large context on every call. That ratio, not the raw total, is your waste compass. Start there.

docs.title: a) Remove tools the agent never uses
docs.text:
Every tool an agent is granted is described in every prompt sent to the model — that's input tokens on every single call, whether the tool is used or not. In the traces, look at which tools an agent actually calls over many runs; anything never called is pure overhead.

Trim the agent's toolNames to only what it uses:

# agents/sre/sre-agent.yaml (illustrative)
spec:
  tools:
    - type: McpServer
      mcpServer:
        toolNames:        # ← keep only the tools this agent actually calls
          - list_pods
          - get_logs
          - dql_query
          # dropped: a dozen k8s tools the SRE agent never invoked

List the tools the agent actually calls straight from the traces, then diff against its granted set:

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and endsWith(service.name, "-sre-agent")
    and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool" and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"
| summarize calls = count(), by:{tool = gen_ai.tool.name}
| sort calls desc

Measure the schema tax directly

Each tool is a JSON schema injected into every prompt. On the reference tenant one captured call_llm request carried 7 tool declarations costing ~1,160 input tokens — about 165 tokens per tool, on every call. The shipped SRE agent (agents/sre/sre-agent.yaml) attaches the Dynatrace MCP server with no toolNames filter (every discovered tool) plus 15 k8s tools. Pin toolNames to the handful the traces prove it uses and you reclaim those tokens on all 1,357 calls — before touching anything else.

The workshop ships that cut ready-made: agents/sre/sre-agent-lean.yaml is the same agent with the Dynatrace MCP pinned to five tools (list_problems, execute_dql, find_entity_by_name, get_kubernetes_events, get_environment_info) instead of the eight read tools the full agent carries. Apply it, send the same prompts, and compare input-token counts in Dynatrace:

applyLeanSreAgent
generateAgentTraffic

Fewer tools → smaller prompts → lower cost on every call. To revert: installAgents.

docs.title: Tool-coverage lookup — the never-called tools, by name
docs.text:
The query above lists the tools an agent did call. The optimization you want is the complement: which granted tools did it never call? Those are the pure-overhead schemas to drop first. Left-join the agent's granted tool set against the tools it actually called, so zero-call tools surface explicitly.

The granted set ships as a lookup table — cluster/dynatrace/optimization/tool-grants.lookup.json — generated from the agents' toolNames. The query below embeds the SRE agent's 15 granted Kubernetes tools inline via data record(...) (so it's self-contained) and lookups the traces for each tool's call count; coalesce(..., 0) turns a never-called tool into a 0, and the verdict column flags the drop candidates:

data record(tool = "k8s_get_resources"),
     record(tool = "k8s_describe_resource"),
     record(tool = "k8s_get_resource_yaml"),
     record(tool = "k8s_get_pod_logs"),
     record(tool = "k8s_get_events"),
     record(tool = "k8s_get_available_api_resources"),
     record(tool = "k8s_get_cluster_configuration"),
     record(tool = "k8s_check_service_connectivity"),
     record(tool = "k8s_apply_manifest"),
     record(tool = "k8s_patch_resource"),
     record(tool = "k8s_scale"),
     record(tool = "k8s_rollout"),
     record(tool = "k8s_label_resource"),
     record(tool = "k8s_annotate_resource"),
     record(tool = "k8s_execute_command")
| lookup [
    fetch spans
    | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent"
        and endsWith(service.name, "-sre-agent")
        and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool"
        and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"
    | summarize calls = count(), by:{tool = gen_ai.tool.name}
  ], sourceField:tool, lookupField:tool, prefix:"called_"
| fieldsAdd calls = coalesce(called_calls, 0)
| fieldsAdd verdict = if(calls == 0, "NEVER CALLED — drop candidate", else: "used")
| fieldsRemove called_tool, called_calls
| sort calls asc

The endsWith(service.name, "-sre-agent") filter here is intentional: coverage is a per-agent question ("which of this agent's granted tools did this agent never call"). To cover another agent, swap the service name and the data record(...) block for that agent's rows from the lookup file. The dashboard's Tool coverage tile and the notebook's tool-coverage cell run exactly this query.

Tool-call count is the headline

The dashboard's top row carries a Tool calls single-value tile (total execute_tool spans) right next to LLM calls — so the never-/rarely-used angle is visible before you even scroll. A tool with zero calls in the coverage table is an unconditional drop; a tool with a handful of calls on a large sample is a rarely-used candidate worth questioning.

docs.title: b) Tighten the system prompt
docs.text: A rambling system prompt is a fixed tax on every request. Shorten it to the essentials; move examples out unless they measurably improve the eval score.

docs.title: c) Fix chatty workflows
docs.text:
In a BMAD run, the span waterfall (module 6) shows how many A2A hops and LLM calls a task took. Redundant hand-offs, an agent that re-reads context it already has, or a loop that retries silently all show up as extra gen_ai spans. Collapse the hops that don't earn their tokens.

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(), inputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens),
    by:{agent = service.name, task = gen_ai.task.id}
| filter llmCalls >= 5
| sort inputTokens desc

Loops are where big agents actually bleed

On the reference tenant the SRE investigator's heaviest task made 7 call_llm hops and re-sent 228,000 input tokens — the same growing context pushed to the model again and again. For an already-lean agent (few tools, tight prompt) this loop re-send, not unused tools, is the dominant cost. The dashboard's loop table ranks these so you fix the worst first.

docs.title: d) Right-size the model per agent
docs.text:
Not every agent needs the most capable model. kagent makes the model a one-line ModelConfig reference, so you can point a cheap, mechanical agent (e.g. a formatter) at a smaller/cheaper model while the reasoning-heavy orchestrator keeps the stronger one. This workshop already defaults the whole crew to DeepSeek for cost; per-agent tuning goes further.

# agents/mcp/00-modelconfig.yaml — the shared workshop-llm (DeepSeek, cost-first)
# Create a second, cheaper ModelConfig and reference it from the agents that
