# don't need the strong model. One field per agent: spec.modelConfig.

docs.title: 3. Prove the win
docs.text:
Open the before/after notebook (deployed above). Its §5 cell measures the one number that moves — average input tokens per LLM call, per agent — and the section time-picker is how you switch the before and after windows. Read the row of the agent you changed:

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(),
    avgInputPerCall    = round(avg(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)),
    medianInputPerCall = round(median(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)),
    totalInputTokens   = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens), by:{service.name}
| sort avgInputPerCall desc

The procedure, in order:

  1. Run the query over a window before the change — record avgInputPerCall.
  2. Make one change (trim tools / tighten prompt / collapse hops / right-size model).
  3. Re-apply and replay the same prompts.
  4. Run the query over the after window and run the dt-evals suite (module 8).

Fill the scorecard from those two runs:

Metric Before After Keep? Avg input tokens / call (§5 notebook) (§5 notebook) — Est. cost / task — — — Eval pass rate (module 8) (module 8) ✅ only if ≥ before

The rule

Ship the change when cost went down and the eval pass rate did not. If quality dropped, revert — the cheaper agent that's wrong is more expensive than the costly one that's right.

docs.title: 4. Make it continuous — the guardian + workflow
docs.text:
Optimization isn't a one-off. Because cost and quality are now both telemetry, the workshop ships two more dtctl-ready artifacts in cluster/dynatrace/optimization/ that turn the optimization loop into an automated gate:

A Site Reliability Guardian (ai-agent-quality-cost.guardian.yaml) — three DQL objectives over the crew's call_llm spans, so a regression fails loudly:

Objective SLI Rule target / warning Cost per LLM call avg input tokens / call ≤ 20,000 / 18,000 Loop efficiency avg hops / task ≤ 5 / 4 Answer substance (quality proxy) avg output tokens / call ≥ 200 / 300 
cd .rendered/optimization        # after renderOptimizationAssets
dtctl create settings -f ai-agent-quality-cost.guardian.yaml \
  --schema app:dynatrace.site.reliability.guardian:guardians --scope environment

The quality proxy backstops the cost cuts — an agent that got "cheaper" by emitting truncated answers trips it. For the full LLM-judge quality gate, pair the guardian with the dt-evals suite (module 8).

A scheduled Workflow (ai-agent-optimization.workflow.yaml) runs that guardian daily over the last 24h (schedule ships disabled — flip trigger.schedule.isActive: true to go continuous):

dtctl create workflow -f ai-agent-optimization.workflow.yaml

No dtctl? Upload .rendered/optimization/ai-agent-optimization.workflow.json from Workflows → Upload. It carries the reference tenant's guardian objectId — after you create your own guardian, repoint it: dtctl get settings --schema app:dynatrace.site.reliability.guardian:guardians -o json --plain | grep -B2 "AI Agent Quality" gives the new objectId; paste it into tasks.run_validation.input.objectId.

Beyond the guardian:

  • Keep the dt-evals suite in CI as a regression + budget gate on every agent change.
  • Watch the dashboard's token-trend tile; the guardian alerts when an agent's tokens-per-call drifts up.
  • Re-rank your agents periodically — usage patterns change, and today's cheap agent is tomorrow's top spender.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• You identified the most expensive agents from real telemetry.
  • You applied at least one concrete cut (unused tools / prompt / hops / model) and proved with evals that quality held while cost fell.
  • You have a repeatable loop — observe → evaluate → change → re-measure — to keep agents cost-efficient in production.

docs.title: You've completed the arc
docs.text:
Why → kagent → cluster → agents → secure → observe → diagnose → evaluate → optimize. You built a full, cost-efficient AI-agent platform on Kubernetes and have the telemetry and evals to keep it that way.

Stuck on anything? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Run of show — the guided 14-step demo
docs.text:
This page is the single, top-to-bottom script for the live demo. It stitches the workshop's modules into one continuous run: configure an agent, investigate a cluster, catch it reading a secret, turn on observability, evaluate the results, and close the observe → evaluate → optimize loop. Each step is deliberately short — just enough to do it — and links to the full module when you want the depth behind it.

How to read this page

Every step has the same shape: What & why (one line), Do it (the exact commands), Apply this (the config or prompt to paste), and Go deeper (the module link). Run the steps in order — later steps depend on the traffic and traces the earlier ones produce.

Prerequisites

The cluster is up and the platform is installed — that's 2 — Setup and 3 — Platform install. After those, the OpenTelemetry Operator, a gateway collector, kagent (clean base, no agents yet), Tetragon, and Phoenix are all running. This walkthrough starts from there.

Two surfaces to keep open

listApps prints the URLs of the kagent UI and Phoenix — both are published through the framework ingress, no port-forward needed. Dynatrace is your tenant.

docs.title: Step 1 — Configure kagent to create an agent
docs.text:
What & why. kagent shipped as a clean runtime in module 3. Here you turn on its built-in Kubernetes tooling, point it at a model, wire the pre-deployed MCP servers, and deploy the SRE agent — one idempotent script does all of it.

Do it. Supply the MCP credentials, then install:

export GH_PAT='github_pat_...'                              # fine-grained, one demo repo
export DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN='dt0s16....'                       # Dynatrace platform token
export DT_ENVIRONMENT='https://<env>.apps.dynatrace.com'    # platform apps URL

installAgents

The script applies, in order: the MCP layer (the shared workshop-llm ModelConfig — DeepSeek — plus the GitHub and Dynatrace MCP tool servers), then the SRE agent, then the BMAD crew. kagent's built-in kagent-tool-server (Kubernetes + networking tools) is already enabled in cluster/kagent/values.yaml.

Apply this. Confirm the tools registered and the agent is Accepted:

kubectl -n kagent get mcpserver,remotemcpserver
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver kagent-tool-server -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get agents          # <prefix>-sre-agent + six <prefix>-bmad-* should be Accepted

Go deeper. 4 — Agents & MCP wiring.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run a simple cluster investigation (SRE agent)
docs.text:
What & why. Prove the agent is alive and can reach its Kubernetes tools with a harmless read-only prompt. This is the "list the pods" baseline — no fault yet.

Do it. Paste the prompt into the <prefix>-sre-agent in the kagent UI (the kagent app — listApps), or send it over A2A:

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List the pods in the kagent namespace and tell me if any are unhealthy."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent

Apply this. You should get a grounded answer naming real pods — the agent called k8s_get_resources, it did not guess. Keep this first run; you'll compare its trace against the re-run in Step 5.

Go deeper. 4 — Agents & MCP wiring.

docs.title: Step 3 — Catch the agent reading a secret (Tetragon)
docs.text:
What & why. The agent is alive — now prove you can see it misbehave. A prompt-injected agent's first move is to grab credentials: the service-account token, a mounted secret, /etc/shadow. Tetragon (installed in module 3) watches the kernel with eBPF, so it catches that read the instant it happens — something admission control can never see because the pod is already running and compliant.

Do it. Apply the ready-made detection policy, then watch the filtered stream:

kubectl apply -f cluster/tetragon/sensitive-file-access.yaml
kubectl -n agent-sandbox get tracingpolicynamespaced   # detect-sensitive-file-access

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact --namespace agent-sandbox

Apply this. In a second terminal, schedule a compliant pod that reads credentials in a loop — /etc/passwd and its own service-account token, exactly what a credential-stealing agent would do. The loop matters: tetra getevents is a live tail, so a one-shot read can land before you are watching; reading every 2 s guarantees the trigger lands inside your watch window.

kubectl -n agent-sandbox run snoop --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"snoop","image":"busybox:1.36","securityContext":{"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":65534,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}},"command":["sh","-c","while true; do cat /etc/passwd /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 2; done"]}]}}' \
  --command -- sh -c 'while true; do cat /etc/passwd /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 2; done'

# when you have seen the event, stop the loop and clean up (leave the policy running)
kubectl -n agent-sandbox delete pod snoop --ignore-not-found

Within a couple of seconds the first terminal prints a process_kprobe line for security_file_permission on the snoop pod, naming cat and the sensitive path — your detection firing. The pod ran clean under Pod Security and was caught reading a credential, because runtime detection sees what admission cannot.

Go deeper. 5 — Secure agents.

docs.title: Step 4 — Show the observability configuration in the collector
docs.text:
What & why. Every answer the agent just gave already emitted spans. The gateway collector is what turns those raw LLM/tool spans into clean, Dynatrace- and Phoenix-ready telemetry — and fans them out to both backends. Open its config so the audience sees there is no magic: it's a normalise + fan-out pipeline.

Do it. Show the live collector and its config:

kubectl get otelcol -n opentelemetry-operator-system          # the gateway collector

Open cluster/otel/collector-gateway.yaml and point at the two things that matter:

processors:
  # Normalise OpenInference / Traceloop LLM attributes onto gen_ai.* semconv
  transform/genai-normalize:
    trace_statements:
      - context: span
        statements:
          - set(attributes["gen_ai.usage.input_tokens"],  attributes["llm.token_count.prompt"])     where ...
          - set(attributes["gen_ai.usage.output_tokens"], attributes["llm.token_count.completion"])  where ...
          - set(attributes["gen_ai.request.model"],       attributes["llm.model_name"])              where ...
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, resourcedetection, resource, transform/genai-normalize, batch]
      exporters:  [otlphttp/dynatrace, otlp/phoenix, debug]   # ← fan-out to BOTH backends

Apply this. The takeaway for the room: whatever instrumentation a tool used (OpenInference, Traceloop, native OTel), the collector rewrites it onto the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* convention — so Dynatrace and Phoenix see the same model, token, and latency fields. The traces pipeline exports to Dynatrace and Phoenix from one place.

Take this home — don't hand-roll OTTL for GenAI. We use a few transform set() statements here because the workshop runs the lighter opentelemetry-collector-k8s image. In your own stack, prefer the purpose-built genainormalizer processor: it ships maintained mappings for OpenInference and OpenLLMetry/Traceloop (token counts, model names, request params, finish reasons) against GenAI semconv v1.40.0 — so you declare sources, not a mapping table you keep in sync.

processors:
  genainormalizer:
    sources:
      - name: openinference
      - name: openllmetry      # Traceloop
        remove_originals: true
# ...then list `genainormalizer` in the traces pipeline instead of transform/genai-normalize

It is a contrib component (Alpha for traces), so using it means running the opentelemetry-collector-contrib image (or a custom OCB build with just this processor) rather than the k8s distro.

Go deeper. 6 — Observe with Dynatrace.

docs.title: Step 5 — Re-run the SRE investigation
docs.text:
What & why. Now that everyone has seen the pipeline, run the agent again — this time to generate traces on purpose. Same agent, slightly broader prompt, so there are fresh runs to open in Phoenix and Dynatrace in the next steps.

Do it.

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List pods in all namespaces and summarise anything not Running."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent

Apply this. Within a few seconds this run is a trace in both backends: an agent.run span wrapping gen_ai LLM calls and k8s tool calls, each carrying input/output token counts and latency. That trace is what Steps 5 and 6 inspect.

Go deeper. 6 — Observe with Dynatrace.

docs.title: Step 6 — Open Phoenix and create one evaluation
docs.text:
What & why. Observability shows what the agent did; evaluation scores whether it was any good. Phoenix is the fast, visual, exploratory judge — and you create and run one LLM-as-a-judge evaluation entirely in its UI, no code.

Do it. Open the phoenix app (listApps) and build the eval in four clicks:

  1. Go to your project's Traces and filter on span_kind == 'LLM'. Each run from Step 5 is an LLM trace; its Input (question) and Output (answer) are visible on the span.
  2. Select the SRE-agent spans → Add to Dataset (each example keeps the span's input + output).
  3. Open that dataset → Evaluators tab → Add evaluator → LLM. In the Playground: pick DeepSeek (the only model in the menu — already keyed when the session has a model key), paste a judge template (hallucination: is the answer grounded? — or relevance: does it answer the question?), map {question}/{answer} to the dataset input/output, Test on one example, Save.
  4. Run the experiment — the judge scores every example server-side.

Apply this. The results table gains a label/score column per evaluator; click a row to read the judge's label + explanation next to the example. A scriptable version (evals/phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py, incl. --from-phoenix to annotate live spans) is the optional CI path. No model key in the session (the in-cluster model only)? Skip to the deterministic grader in module 8 Part C.

Go deeper. 8 — Evaluate · Part A (Phoenix).

docs.title: Step 7 — Open Dynatrace: traces + AI Observability
docs.text:
What & why. Same spans, production-grade backend. Dynatrace adds estimated cost, a full distributed-trace waterfall, and correlation with cluster health — the signals that drive the workshop's cost-efficiency theme.

Do it. In your tenant (…apps.dynatrace.com), open the app launcher and go to AI & LLM Observability.

Apply this. Walk the four questions on one agent, then open a single trace:

Question Where to look How much does a run cost? token usage × model price → estimated cost per request Where does the latency go? span waterfall: model time vs tool time vs A2A hops Is it reliable? error rate + failure spans Is it efficient? tokens per task, tool calls per task, retries

Because every agent shares the workshop-llm (DeepSeek) ModelConfig, you'll see one DeepSeek endpoint with call volume, tokens, latency, error rate, and cost. Click into a request to see gen_ai LLM spans and k8s tool spans nested under agent.run.

Go deeper. 6 — Observe with Dynatrace.

docs.title: Step 8 — Create an evaluation using dt-evals
docs.text:
What & why. Phoenix was exploratory; dt-evals is the CI-friendly path. It samples gen_ai.* spans straight from Dynatrace, masks PII, scores each with a judge, and writes the results back as bizevents next to the rest of your telemetry — so a low score is one click from the trace that caused it.

Do it. Put the credentials in evals/.env, then run the wrapper:

cd evals/dt-evals
./run-dt-eval.sh          # renders the config with your env, then runs validate + run

The .env needs a dedicated DYNATRACE_API_TOKEN (dt0c01 with storage:spans:read + storage:events:write); the tenant comes from DT_ENVIRONMENT and the judge key from your session (room-password proxy or DEEPSEEK_API_KEY). DT_EVAL_SERVICE defaults to ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent; confirm that service name with DQL rather than guessing it:

fetch spans, from: now() - 2h
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}")
| filter isNotNull(gen_ai.operation.name) or isNotNull(gen_ai.request.model)
| summarize span_count = count(), by: { service.name }
| sort span_count desc

Apply this. The shipped config enables relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, coherence, toxicity, and prompt-injection metrics, and sets thresholds that make the run exit non-zero on a breach — a ready-made CI gate.

Go deeper. 8 — Evaluate · Part B (dt-evals).

docs.title: Step 9 — Run the BMAD investigation
docs.text:
What & why. So far it's been the single SRE agent. Now show the other side of the platform: the BMAD crew — a six-member orchestrated workflow (analyst → PM → architect → developer → QA, driven by the orchestrator). A BMAD run is a long, multi-hop trace — exactly the kind of workload the optimize steps later target.

Do it. Send the orchestrator a task (kagent UI → <prefix>-bmad-orchestrator, or A2A):

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Build a simple Todo app in <owner>/<repo>. Run the full BMAD workflow and open a PR."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-bmad-orchestrator

Apply this. In the trace you'll see the orchestrator's A2A hops to each crew member as nested spans, and the developer agent using the GitHub MCP tools to open issues, push a branch, and raise a PR. This is the multi-agent run whose hop-count and token spend you'll scrutinise in Step 13.

Go deeper. 4 — Agents & MCP wiring.

docs.title: Step 10 — Review the Phoenix evaluation
docs.text:
What & why. Close the loop you opened in Step 6: read the scores. Phoenix is where you discover failure modes interactively.

Do it. In the phoenix app (listApps), reopen the dataset you scored in Step 6 and look at its experiment results. Each example row carries the judge's label and score (hallucination / relevance). Sort by score to surface the weakest answers, and click a row to read the judge's explanation alongside that example's input and output.

Apply this. For the SRE agent the questions that matter: did it identify the right pod, call the right tool (not guess), and stay grounded in real tool output (no hallucinated pod names)? If you also ran the optional script, the same numbers land in evals/phoenix/out/phoenix_eval_results.csv and as labels on the live spans.

Go deeper. 8 — Evaluate · Part A (Phoenix).

docs.title: Step 11 — Review the dt-evals results
docs.text:
What & why. The dt-evals run from Step 8 wrote its scores into Dynatrace as bizevents. Read them with DQL — this is the queryable, alertable, CI-gated view of quality.

Do it. In a Dynatrace Notebook:

fetch bizevents
| filter event.type == "gen_ai.evaluation.result"
| filter service.name == "<prefix>-sre-agent"   // <prefix>: echo $WORKSHOP_PREFIX
| summarize avg(toDouble(gen_ai.evaluation.score.value)), by: { gen_ai.evaluation.name }

Apply this. You get an average score per evaluator (relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, …). Because the scores live next to the spans, any low score is one click from the trace, prompt, and tool calls that produced it — and the run already exited non-zero if a threshold was breached, which is your CI gate.

Go deeper. 8 — Evaluate · Part B · Read the scores.

docs.title: Step 12 — Deploy the notebook
docs.text:
What & why. You've measured cost (Step 7) and quality (Steps 10–11). The optimize module ships a ready-made Dynatrace notebook that computes every optimization signal from your crew's gen_ai.* spans — deploy it so the next DQL steps run against a real surface, not a blank page.

Do it.

renderOptimizationAssets     # scope every DQL to workshop.attendee == your prefix
deployOptimizationAssets     # dtctl: read-the-run notebook, dashboard, before/after notebook

No platform token in the session? Upload the .json files from .rendered/optimization/ in Dynatrace (Notebooks / Dashboards → Upload).

Apply this. The notebook — AI Agent Optimization — before/after — is the observe → find → change → re-measure → keep/revert walkthrough, one runnable DQL cell per step. Its §5 cell measures the single number optimization moves: average input tokens per LLM call, per agent. Start with the read-the-run notebook if you want to page through one run before cutting anything.

Go deeper. 9 — Optimize · deploy the surfaces.

docs.title: Step 13 — Build DQL queries: tool usage + token utilization
docs.text:
What & why. This is the heart of optimization. Two questions answer "where is the waste?": which tools does an agent actually call (anything granted but never called is pure prompt overhead), and how many tokens is each agent burning (especially the input:output ratio, your waste compass).

Do it — token utilization (rank agents by spend):

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(),
    inputTokens  = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens),
    outputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens),
    by:{agent = service.name}
| fieldsAdd totalTokens = inputTokens + outputTokens,
    inOutRatio      = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / outputTokens, decimals: 1),
    avgInputPerCall = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / llmCalls)
| sort totalTokens desc

Do it — tool usage (what an agent really calls):

fetch spans
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") and service.namespace == "kagent"
    and endsWith(service.name, "-sre-agent")
    and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool" and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"
| summarize calls = count(), by:{tool = gen_ai.tool.name}
| sort calls desc

Apply this. Diff the tools the traces prove an agent uses against the tool set it was granted — every unused tool is a JSON schema injected into every prompt (~165 input tokens per tool, on every call). A high input:output ratio (e.g. 38:1) means the model re-reads a large context each call — that, not the raw total, is where to cut. This ranking is the raw material for the cuts in module 9.

Go deeper. 9 — Optimize · the four cuts.

docs.title: Step 14 — Deploy the workflow
docs.text:
What & why. Optimization isn't a one-off. Because cost and quality are now both telemetry, the last artifact makes the loop continuous: a scheduled Dynatrace workflow runs a Site Reliability Guardian daily, so a cost or quality regression fails loudly on its own.

Do it. Deploy the guardian, then the workflow that runs it:

cd .rendered/optimization     # rendered by renderOptimizationAssets
dtctl create settings -f ai-agent-quality-cost.guardian.yaml \
  --schema app:dynatrace.site.reliability.guardian:guardians --scope environment
dtctl create workflow -f ai-agent-optimization.workflow.yaml

Apply this. The guardian holds three DQL objectives over the crew's call_llm spans — cost per call (avg input tokens ≤ 20k), loop efficiency (avg hops ≤ 5), and an answer-substance quality proxy (avg output tokens ≥ 200) so an agent that got "cheaper" by truncating answers trips the gate. The workflow ships with its schedule disabled; flip trigger.schedule.isActive: true to run it over the last 24h every day.

Go deeper. 9 — Optimize · make it continuous.

docs.title: You've run the whole show
docs.text: In fourteen steps you configured an agent, investigated a cluster, caught it reading a secret with runtime security, exposed the telemetry pipeline, evaluated the results two ways, and closed the observe → evaluate → optimize loop with queries and automation that keep the crew cost-efficient. For the depth behind any step, follow its Go deeper link — and when something misbehaves, the Troubleshooting page collects the common fixes per module.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: A single place for the problems attendees hit most, grouped by module. Each component also has a deeper README under cluster/ and agents/.

docs.title: First, the three catch-all checks
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A | grep -vE 'Running|Completed'   # anything not healthy
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30
kubectl top nodes; kubectl top pods -A | sort -k4 -h | tail   # CPU/memory headroom

Most failures are resources or secrets

On a 2-core/4GB Codespace the stack will not fit. Use 4-core / 16 GB or larger (see .devcontainer/DECISIONS.md). The second most common cause is a missing/misscoped credential — run variablesNeeded DT_ENVIRONMENT:true DT_INGEST_TOKEN:true DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN:true (names only, never values).

docs.title: Module 2 — Setup
docs.text:
Cluster not reachable / kubectl hangs. Re-create or restart the cluster:

bash .devcontainer/postCreate.sh     # full, idempotent bootstrap
bash .devcontainer/postStart.sh      # just restart the cluster after a resume
kubectl cluster-info

Secrets not detected. Codespace secrets only apply to codespaces created after they're set. Set them, then rebuild the container (Command Palette → Codespaces: Rebuild Container), and verify:

variablesNeeded DT_ENVIRONMENT:true DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN:true DT_INGEST_TOKEN:true DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN:true   # presence only, never values

docs.title: Module 3 — Platform install
docs.text:
The install reports warnings but doesn't crash. That's by design — missing secrets degrade gracefully (a component is skipped or warns). Re-run after fixing the secret: installPlatform.

Dynatrace: no data on the tenant. Check DT_TENANT_URL / DT_API_TOKEN and token scopes (openTelemetryTrace.ingest, metrics.ingest, logs.ingest, plus the k8s-monitoring scopes). The DynaKube secret name must equal the DynaKube name (dynakube).

kubectl get dynakube -n dynatrace
kubectl -n dynatrace get pods            # operator, webhook, activegate Ready

OTel operator hangs applying the collector CR. The operator must use its self-signed webhook cert (autoGenerateCert), already set in otel/operator-values.yaml. installOtelGateway retries the CR for ~100 s while the webhook registers.

kubectl -n opentelemetry-operator-system get otelcol
kubectl -n opentelemetry-operator-system logs deploy/opentelemetry-operator

docs.title: Tetragon not Ready or CrashLooping
docs.text:
k3d/kind nodes share the Codespace host kernel; Tetragon needs BTF and probe permissions.

kubectl -n tetragon logs ds/tetragon -c tetragon
kubectl -n tetragon get pods
  • Confirm host BTF exists: ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux.
  • Fallback: run observation-only (no enforcement). TracingPolicy with Sigkill may be unavailable on a restricted host kernel — document it as a known Codespace limitation rather than blocking the workshop. See cluster/tetragon/README.md.

docs.title: Tetragon is Ready but the sensitive-file policy fires no events
docs.text:
You applied sensitive-file-access.yaml, started the getevents watch, and launched the snoop pod — but the stream stays empty. The Tetragon pods are healthy, so this is almost never a kernel problem. Work down this ladder:

1. Confirm the policy actually loaded, not just that kubectl apply succeeded. apply only means the apiserver stored the custom resource — the Tetragon agent still has to load the kprobe selectors into the kernel, and it can silently reject the policy at load time (it only logs a warn, and leaves the kprobe un-attached, so no event ever fires). This is the single most common cause. Check the per-policy state:

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra tracingpolicy list

STATE: enabled is good. A load_error state (or an ERROR column) means the kprobe never attached. Look at why in the agent log:

kubectl -n tetragon logs ds/tetragon -c tetragon --tail=500 \
  | grep -iE "tracing policy|detect-sensitive-file-access"

A line like ReturnArgAction type 'Post' unsupported means you are running a stale copy of the policy from before the fix in this repo. Re-apply the policy from this repository (the fix removed returnArgAction: Post):

kubectl delete -f cluster/tetragon/sensitive-file-access.yaml --ignore-not-found
kubectl apply  -f cluster/tetragon/sensitive-file-access.yaml

2. Give the kprobe a few seconds to attach, and keep the read in a loop. tetra getevents is a live tail — it shows only events that happen after it attaches and never replays history. After apply, wait ~10 s for the agent to load the selectors, and make sure the snoop pod reads in a loop (the workshop one-liner does: while true; do cat … ; sleep 2; done). A one-shot cat can fire before the kprobe is live and you will see nothing.

3. Isolate the --namespace filter. Drop it and watch the raw stream (or filter by pod) while the loop runs — this tells you whether the policy fired at all vs. whether the namespace filter dropped the event (pod metadata can take a few seconds to resolve):

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra getevents -o compact --pods snoop

4. Read the output correctly. The compact renderer prints a security_file_permission file read as a read action line — not the literal word "kprobe":

📚 read    agent-sandbox/snoop /bin/cat /etc/passwd

If you see process/exit lines for snoop but no read line, the pod is running but the policy is not loaded — go back to step 1. A reproducible end-to-end check lives in cluster/tetragon/validate-live.sh.

Phoenix not Ready. It uses one RWO PVC with strategy: Recreate — never two pods on the same volume.

kubectl -n phoenix get pods
kubectl -n phoenix logs deploy/phoenix

docs.title: Module 4 — Agents & MCP wiring
docs.text:
A RemoteMCPServer isn't Accepted / discoveredTools is empty. The tool server couldn't start or authenticate. Check the token and the server pod:

kubectl -n kagent get mcpserver,remotemcpserver
kubectl -n kagent describe remotemcpserver dynatrace-mcp-remote
kubectl -n kagent logs deploy/kagent-controller
  • GH_PAT must be a fine-grained PAT scoped to the demo repo (Contents / Issues / Pull requests RW).
  • Dynatrace MCP needs the platform token (dt0s16.*) and DT_ENVIRONMENT (the .apps.dynatrace.com URL) — distinct from the module 3 OTLP DT_API_TOKEN.

An Agent isn't Accepted. Usually a bad ModelConfig or missing model secret.

kubectl -n kagent get agents
kubectl -n kagent describe agent ${WORKSHOP_PREFIX}-sre-agent
kubectl -n kagent get secret kagent-deepseek    # model key present?

A2A prompt times out. Multi-hop BMAD runs take minutes — keep the client timeout generous (curl -m 300). Watch progress in the kagent UI (the kagent app — listApps).

docs.title: Module 5 — Secure
docs.text:
A pod won't schedule into agent-sandbox. That's PSA restricted working — pods must be non-root, drop ALL caps, no privilege escalation, seccomp RuntimeDefault. Add the required securityContext (see the examples in module 5).

A sandboxed pod can't reach a service. Expected — the default-deny NetworkPolicy allows egress only to DNS and the OTel gateway. Add an explicit egress rule if a workload legitimately needs more.

docs.title: Module 6 — Observe
docs.text:
No agent traces in Dynatrace. First generate traffic (send a prompt). Then check the pipeline end to end:

kubectl -n opentelemetry-operator-system get otelcol
kubectl -n opentelemetry-operator-system logs deploy/otel-gateway-collector | tail -40

Confirm kagent otel.tracing points at otel-gateway-collector.opentelemetry-operator-system.svc:4317, and that the tenant/token scopes include openTelemetryTrace.ingest.

Gateway logs connection refused to phoenix.phoenix.svc...:4317 at startup. Benign and self-healing — the gateway starts before Phoenix is Ready and retries. Once Phoenix is up the otlp/phoenix exporter connects and the warnings stop. Only investigate if it persists after kubectl -n phoenix get pods shows Phoenix Running.

otlphttp/k8sattributes/resourcedetection deprecation warnings

"otlphttp" alias is deprecated; use "otlp_http" and the matching resource_detection / k8s_attributes lines are informational in collector 0.161+. The old aliases still work — not an error, no action needed.

Phoenix shows the trace but Input / Output are empty. The gateway copies the kagent/ADK gcp.vertex.agent.llm_request / llm_response attributes onto the OpenInference input.value / output.value keys Phoenix reads. A collector from before that change shows bare spans — re-render it with installOtelGateway.

docs.title: Module 7 — Diagnose
docs.text:
run.sh inject 12 exits 2 with "is opt-in … needs the astroshop-lite app". Scenario 12 is the opt-in app scenario. Either skip it (run 01–03) or deploy the demo once with a single Helm install (the platform stack is already up): deployOtelDemoLight. The yellow [ warn ] + cyan [ info ] lines are guidance, not a failure. Scenarios 01–03 have no such dependency.

unknown/ambiguous scenario id. Pass a numeric prefix (01, 12) or the full dir name (01-crashloopbackoff); run bash scenarios/run.sh list to see valid ids.

The injected pod never appears. run.sh applies into the workshop-faults namespace — watch there, not default: kubectl get pods -n workshop-faults. A fail-closed allowlist rejects (exit 2) any manifest referencing a platform namespace before applying, so if inject refused, check the manifest's namespace: is workshop-faults.

The agent cites the wrong failure class (e.g. "OOMKilled" for the crash loop). That's a graded fail, not a tooling bug — the infra scenarios sit on distinct evidence channels on purpose. Re-run and, if it persists, confirm the sre-agent has its k8s read tools (k8s_get_pod_logs, k8s_get_events) from module 4.

Cleanup left something behind. bash scenarios/run.sh cleanup <id> is idempotent; for infra scenarios it deletes the whole workshop-faults namespace. Re-run it, or kubectl delete ns workshop-faults --ignore-not-found.

docs.title: Module 8 — Evaluate
docs.text:
Phoenix UI empty. Same root cause as "no traces" above — fix the OTel pipeline, then re-send prompts. Confirm the forward:

listApps    # the phoenix URL

dt-evals can't resolve dependencies. Run inside evals/ with uv:

cd evals && uv sync

The concrete suite ships in module 8 — evals/dt-evals/workshop-agents.dt-eval.yaml plus the Phoenix scripts are on main.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text:
• Re-run the idempotent installers — they reconcile, they don't duplicate: installPlatform, installAgents.
  • Tear down and start clean: deleteCluster && startK3dCluster && installPlatform && installAgents.
  • Open an issue on the workshop repo.
